metadata.title: Further, But Better
metadata.note: STEM/AI explainer on Kehinde's own quantlab repo (ML-04). The ONE idea: rounding error is a move in weight space, but damage is measured in loss space, so the better method moves the weights FURTHER and hurts LESS. B03 is his own Manim animation, re-rendered at 4K from assets/manim_gptq.py rather than upscaled. Every figure measured across 34 evaluations on one fixed wikitext-2 protocol.

props.command: I implemented three post-training quantization methods on GPT-2 from their papers and measured 34 configurations on one fixed protocol. The winning method ends up with weights FURTHER from the originals than naive rounding, yet its outputs are closer. Help me explain why moving further can hurt less.
output: the distance is not the damage

beats.new_visual_element: Four bits, eight times smaller, a nine percent tax
beats.narration: Here is the trade in one picture. The full-size model scores twenty-six point two on a standard text benchmark, where lower is better. Squeeze every number down to four bits and the best method scores twenty-eight point five. That is eight times less memory for about a nine percent quality tax. Push to two bits and everything collapses.

beats.new_visual_element: Rounding in a tilted valley (Kehinde's own Manim)
beats.narration: So why does one method survive where the others do not. Picture the error as a landscape. Some directions are flat, you can move a long way and nothing happens. Others are steep. Naive rounding snaps every number to the nearest step and takes whatever hit it gets. The better method rounds one number, then slides the ones it has not touched yet to soak up that error before they are rounded.

beats.new_visual_element: Further by distance, closer by output
beats.narration: And here is the part I did not expect. Measured as raw distance, the better method is worse. Its weights end up two and a half times further from the originals than naive rounding. But measured by what actually comes out of the model, its outputs are twice as accurate. It deliberately moves further in order to land somewhere flatter.

beats.new_visual_element: Was I comparing methods, or comparing settings?
beats.narration: I also got my own comparison wrong the first time, and it is worth admitting. My version of the good method used one setting, and my version of the naive method used a different one. So what I had actually measured was not method against method, it was setting against setting. The setting was doing the winning. I rebuilt it so both sides matched, and only then did the comparison mean anything.

data.question: One side won. But what actually won?

branches.label: THE SETTING
branches.detail: One side had a better one.

resolver.label: MATCH EVERYTHING ELSE
resolver.detail: Change one axis at a time, or the conclusion is half accounting.

beats.narration: So what I would take from thirty-four evaluations. Measure the thing you actually care about, not the thing that is easy to measure. Change one variable at a time, or you will not know what won. And when a published recipe underperforms, check whether you are running the whole recipe, because the paper searched a setting I had left fixed.

show.event: Artifact card opens, titled 'What 34 evaluations taught me'
Five numbered lines stagger in
The last line holds longest

artifactLines: Distance from the original is not damage to the answer.
Measure the output, not the thing that is easy to measure.
Change one axis at a time or the winner is half accounting.
A recipe that underperforms may just be half-followed.
Report the configs that failed. They are the honest part.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the viewer's prompt typed
beats.narration: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a benchmark you trust, whether it is yours or one you read, and list every setting that differs between the things being compared. Not just the method, everything: the data, the preprocessing, the tuning budget, the hardware. Then tell me which differences could explain the result on their own. Do not tell me which option is better. Tell me what else changed. Most benchmarks I have seen, including my own first one, lose on that question.

props.command: Take a benchmark comparing two methods, mine or one from a paper. List every setting that differs between the two arms: data, preprocessing, tuning budget, scale granularity, hardware, evaluation protocol. Then tell me which of those differences could produce the reported result on its own. Do not tell me which method is better. Tell me what else changed.
